Climate Change. Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, primarily driven by human activities since the onset of industrialization. The phenomenon accelerates ice loss at the poles, reshapes weather systems, and threatens ecosystems and human societies worldwide. It has become central to both scientific inquiry and political discourse, crystallizing in the late twentieth century as the defining environmental challenge.

Temperature has risen approximately one point one degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, with the majority of warming occurring in recent decades. Projections suggest reaching one point five to two degrees Celsius by twenty fifty under current trajectories. Climate change is primarily caused by greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, and industrial agriculture. Carbon dioxide concentration has risen from two hundred eighty parts per million to over four hundred twenty parts per million.

Observable effects include melting glaciers, rising sea levels at approximately three to four millimeters per year, ocean acidification, and intensifying extreme weather events like hurricanes and droughts. Antarctica and Greenland ice sheets are leading indicators of warming trends and potential irreversible tipping points. Their collapse could raise sea levels catastrophically. Glaciers on peaks like Mount Kilimanjaro have retreated dramatically over the past century, visible markers of planetary warming accessible to scientific measurement.

Climate change emerged as a major political and cultural force in the nineteen nineties, with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in nineteen ninety-two and later the Paris Agreement in twenty fifteen. Al Gore became the public face of climate activism after his tenure as Vice President, making it his signature cause. His documentary amplified scientific consensus to mass audiences. Climate connects to Antarctica as the continent most vulnerable to warming and its ice-sheet collapse implications, to Mount Kilimanjaro whose shrinking glaciers serve as iconic visual proof, to Al Gore as the environmentalist and former vice president who made climate action his defining legacy, to the Industrial Revolution as the historical period whose energy systems initiated the greenhouse effect, and to the United States as both a major emitter and arena for climate policy debate.
